objectives: Compare the Big Five mass extinctions — causes, magnitudes, + ecospace effects.
Explain recovery dynamics — disaster faunas, dead clades walking, refilling timescales.
Situate the ongoing 6th extinction (Pimm-Brooks; Anthropocene) relative to deep-time precedents.

slides.title: The Big Five: Raup-Sepkoski mass extinctions
slides.body:
**Raup + Sepkoski 1982** *Science* — the canonical paper. Using Sepkoski's compendium of marine family + genus first + last appearances through the Phanerozoic, Raup + Sepkoski identified **five statistically distinct extinction peaks** above the background rate: the **Big Five**. They are (in chronological order):

**1. End-Ordovician (Ordovician-Silurian, ~445 Mya)**.
- **Magnitude**: ~85% of marine species lost; ~57% of genera.
- **Cause**: rapid glaciation as Gondwana drifted over the South Pole; sea-level fall (~100 m), habitat loss; followed by post-glacial sea-level rise + anoxia. Two-pulse extinction (~447 + ~444 Mya).
- **Mechanism**: cooling reduced tropical-shelf habitat by ~95%; many shallow-water taxa with narrow temperature tolerance went extinct (graptolites, brachiopods, trilobites).
- **Survivors**: deep-water + cold-tolerant taxa; conodonts mostly survived; corals + crinoids decimated then rebuilt.

**2. Late Devonian (~372-359 Mya)**.
- **Magnitude**: ~75% of marine species over a series of pulses (Kellwasser ~372 Mya, Hangenberg ~359 Mya); ~50% genera.
- **Cause**: complex + multifactorial. **Ocean anoxia** is the dominant signal; tied to expanding land plants drawing down CO₂, atmospheric cooling, + sea-level changes; possible large igneous province activity. The Hangenberg event (basal Carboniferous) is now considered the most severe — eliminating jawed-fish placoderms.
- **Survivors**: terrestrial tetrapods that had just evolved (*Acanthostega*, *Ichthyostega*) actually survived + diversified afterward. Placoderms disappeared completely.

**3. End-Permian (Permian-Triassic, the 'Great Dying', ~251.9 Mya)**.
- **Magnitude**: **~96% marine species; ~70% terrestrial vertebrate species** — the largest extinction in Earth's history. Knocked out trilobites permanently, rugose + tabulate corals, fusulinid forams, eurypterids.
- **Cause**: **Siberian Traps**, an enormous flood-basalt province (~7 × 10⁶ km³ over ~600 kyr) erupting through coal + carbonate at the same time. Outgassed CO₂ + SO₂ + HCl + Hg → global warming (~10 °C tropical + polar), ocean acidification, ocean anoxia + euxinia (H₂S), terrestrial UV damage from ozone loss. **Doug Erwin** (Smithsonian) *Extinction: How Life on Earth Nearly Ended 250 Million Years Ago* (2006); Erwin 2015 *Science*; Burgess + Bowring 2015 PNAS dated the entire extinction to <60 kyr.
- **Recovery**: 5-30 Myr; *Lystrosaurus* was the great disaster taxon on land, ammonites + brachiopods recovered slowly. The Modern marine fauna (Sepkoski) emerged.

**4. End-Triassic (Triassic-Jurassic, ~201.4 Mya)**.
- **Magnitude**: ~70-75% of marine species, including conodonts (after 280 Myr).
- **Cause**: **Central Atlantic Magmatic Province (CAMP)** — a large igneous province coincident with Pangaea breakup, with CO₂ + climate effects similar to (but smaller than) the Siberian Traps. Marzoli et al. 1999 dated CAMP at 201 Mya, matching the extinction.
- **Survivors + radiation**: dinosaurs, which had originated in the Triassic, exploded into the vacated niches in the Early Jurassic — the **Mesozoic dinosaur dominance** is a direct ecological consequence.

**5. End-Cretaceous (Cretaceous-Paleogene = K-Pg, formerly K-T, ~66.0 Mya)**.
- **Magnitude**: ~75% of species; all **non-avian dinosaurs**, pterosaurs, mosasaurs, ammonites, ~93% of mammals.
- **Cause**: **Chicxulub impact**. **Walter Alvarez** (UC Berkeley) + **Luis Alvarez** (his physicist father, Nobel 1968) + Frank Asaro + Helen Michel — **Alvarez et al. 1980** *Science* — identified a global **iridium anomaly** in K-Pg boundary clay (~30× background, indicating extraterrestrial origin). Proposed asteroid impact. **Alan Hildebrand** + Penfield + Camargo + others in **1991** identified the **Chicxulub crater** (180-200 km diameter, ~66.0 Mya) buried under the Yucatán; shocked quartz, microspherules, tsunami deposits in K-Pg clays match impact origin. **Schulte et al. 2010** *Science* — a 41-author consensus paper reviewed evidence; concluded impact alone is sufficient + the timing matches the extinction.
- **Compounding factors**: the **Deccan Traps** (India) flood-basalt province (eruption ~67-65 Mya) added climate stress + likely weakened ecosystems before the impact. **Schoene 2019** + **Sprain 2019** debated whether Deccan was main driver or accompaniment; modern consensus is Chicxulub was the proximate cause, with Deccan as significant accompaniment. **Tanis site** (Hell Creek, North Dakota, DePalma 2019 PNAS) — exquisite Lagerstätte preserving fish + fossils killed within hours of the impact.
- **Survivors**: small placental + marsupial mammals, crocodilians, turtles, birds (avian dinosaurs), insects. The **mammal-dominated Cenozoic** is the direct consequence.

**Beyond the Big Five**:
- **Cambrian-Ordovician boundary** + **Late Ordovician (sometimes counted as one of the Big Five)**.
- **Late Cambrian (e.g., Trempealeauan)** + **End-Guadalupian (Capitanian, ~260 Mya)** — increasingly viewed as a 'Big Sixth' (Stanley + Yang).
- **Late Eocene** (~34 Mya) + **Pliocene-Pleistocene** + **Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum (PETM, ~56 Mya)** — major perturbations but not classical mass extinctions.

The Big Five are not all alike. The end-Permian is biological apocalypse via volcanic-climate feedback; the K-Pg is impact-driven catastrophe; the Ordovician is glaciation; the Devonian is anoxic + complex; the Triassic-Jurassic is volcanic-climate. The diversity of causes is a major paleobiological lesson: **mass extinction is not one phenomenon, but several distinct catastrophes with different signatures**.

slides.title: Recovery: disaster faunas + dead clades walking + ecospace refilling
slides.body:
What happens *after* a mass extinction? Recovery is not just re-evolution — it has its own dynamics + signature patterns.

**Disaster taxa** — opportunistic, generalist, weedy species that proliferate immediately post-extinction by filling vacated ecospace before normal communities recover. Classic example: ***Lystrosaurus***, a dicynodont synapsid (mammal-ancestor relative) that came through the Permian-Triassic extinction + briefly dominated Early Triassic terrestrial faunas globally — >90% of Early Triassic tetrapods in some sites. *Lystrosaurus* was a barrel-bodied medium-sized herbivore (~50-100 kg) that was probably tolerant of low oxygen + tough vegetation. Other disaster taxa:
- Post-K-Pg: ferns ('fern spike' in post-impact strata — ferns are early colonizers, equivalent of disturbance taxa); the gastropod *Provannidae*; the mammal *Purgatorius* (one of the earliest known placental mammals).
- Post-PT: *Claraia* (a bivalve that bloomed in low-oxygen post-extinction Triassic seas).
- Post-end-Ordovician: graptolites that survived the cold-water refugium expanded back.

**Dead clades walking** — **David Jablonski 2002** *PNAS*. Some clades survive the extinction in low numbers but are *functionally extinct* — they linger for Myrs but never recover dominance + ultimately disappear. Examples:
- Trilobites declined from the Devonian onward + finally died at end-Permian — they were essentially dead clades walking after end-Devonian.
- Crinoids survived the Permian-Triassic but the Paleozoic crinoid fauna (stalked, stationary, deep-water) was replaced by very different Mesozoic + Modern crinoid faunas (mostly comatulids — feather stars).
- Brachiopods survived but were ecologically displaced by bivalves; the post-PT brachiopod fauna is a Modern relict, ~5% of pre-PT diversity.

**Ecospace refilling** — recovery is *uneven* + *non-isotropic*. Filling depends on (a) survivor ecology, (b) ecological vacancies, (c) functional novelty. Empirical patterns:
- **Rapid recovery of generalists, slow recovery of specialists**. Filter-feeders, deep-water specialists, top predators recover last.
- **5-30 Myr to full diversity recovery** — Erwin's empirical generalization. **Marine genus diversity** typically takes ~10-20 Myr to return to pre-extinction levels; some ecosystem properties (top predators, large body sizes) take much longer.
- **Bias toward new evolutionary types**: mass extinctions are not just catastrophes — they are major opportunities for evolutionary innovation. The end-Permian eliminated Paleozoic fauna + opened ecospace for Mesozoic marine reptiles, ammonites, modern bony fish + sharks (Mesozoic Marine Revolution, Vermeij 1977). K-Pg eliminated dinosaurs + opened ecospace for placental mammal diversification (Eocene radiation; horse + cetacean + primate lineages all post-date the K-Pg).

**Recovery timescales** — quantitative estimates from Sepkoski, Alroy, Erwin, Knoll:
- **End-Permian recovery**: 5 Myr for first-wave recovery (Early Triassic disaster fauna); 10 Myr for genus diversity to return to pre-extinction levels (Anisian Stage, ~245 Mya); 30 Myr for full ecological reorganization + return of complex reefs (Late Triassic).
- **K-Pg recovery**: ~5-10 Myr for diversity recovery; Cenozoic mammalian + bird diversity exceeds pre-K-Pg amniote diversity by mid-Eocene (~50 Mya).
- **Erwin 2001 *PNAS*** + **Erwin 2015 *Science*** synthesize recovery theory.

**Refugia + niche construction** — some species survive in refugia (deep marine, subterranean, polar, equatorial) + later re-expand. Niche construction (Odling-Smee + Laland) means survivors actively reshape post-extinction ecosystems.

Mass extinctions are **macroevolutionary inflection points**: they reset trajectory + open novel pathways. The history of life is partly a history of these resets — without the K-Pg there are no humans; without the PT there is no Mesozoic; without the Late Devonian there are no terrestrial vertebrates. The pattern of biodiversity through deep time *is* the pattern of these resets.

slides.title: The 6th extinction: Anthropocene defaunation
slides.body:
Are we currently in a mass extinction? **Yes — the consensus among ecologists + paleontologists is that the **6th mass extinction** is underway**, with extinction rates ~100-1000× background.

**Quantitative evidence**:
- **Pimm + Brooks** + colleagues (1995+ + 2014 *Science*): estimated background extinction rates from the fossil record at ~1 species per million species-years (E/MSY). Modern measured extinctions are ~100-1000× this — 1000× would put us in mass-extinction territory.
- **Ceballos et al. 2015 *Science Advances*** + 2017: vertebrate extinction rates ~100× background even using a *conservative* background estimate.
- **IUCN Red List**: ~28% of all assessed species are threatened. Mammals: ~25%; amphibians: ~40% (~half of declines from the chytrid fungus epidemic, Berger + Speare 1998+); birds: ~13%; corals: ~33%.
- **Dirzo + Galetti et al. 2014 *Science* 'Defaunation in the Anthropocene'** — synthesized the data on global animal population declines. Vertebrate populations dropped ~60% since 1970 (WWF Living Planet Index 2020). Large-bodied vertebrates have suffered the steepest declines.
- **Insect declines**: Hallmann 2017 *PLOS One* — 76% biomass decline in German nature reserves over 27 years. Mounting evidence for global insect collapse.

**Causes** (HIPPO acronym — Habitat destruction + Invasive species + Pollution + Population (human) + Overharvesting):
- **Habitat destruction**: 50% of habitable land already converted to agriculture; tropical deforestation ongoing.
- **Climate change**: ~1.2 °C warming since pre-industrial; coral bleaching, range shifts, phenological mismatches.
- **Pollution**: pesticides (neonicotinoids on insects), plastics, light pollution, nitrogen deposition.
- **Invasive species**: introduced predators + competitors on islands (rats on islands killed many bird species).
- **Overharvesting**: marine fisheries, wildlife trade, megafauna.
- **Disease**: chytrid fungus, white-nose syndrome (bats), now bird flu strains.

**The Anthropocene**:
- **Jan Zalasiewicz** + the **Anthropocene Working Group** (AWG): formally proposed the Anthropocene as an epoch with base ~1952 (plutonium fallout from atmospheric nuclear testing + correlated stratigraphic markers — plastic fragments, fly ash, novel chemicals, ¹⁴C bomb spike). Proposed GSSP at Crawford Lake, Ontario (varved sediments) in 2023.
- **March 2024**: ICS Subcommission on Quaternary Stratigraphy voted **against** ratification (24-of-37 against, after a 60% no-vote requirement). The Anthropocene remains an *informal* term but widely used in geology, ecology, climate science, + social science. Continued advocacy by Zalasiewicz + Steffen + Crutzen + Williams + Waters.
- Whether or not formally ratified, the empirical reality of geological-scale human impact (atmospheric CO₂, sediment fluxes, climate, biota, novel materials) is uncontested. The Anthropocene is a useful concept regardless of chronostratigraphic status.

**Comparing to deep-time extinctions**: the 6th extinction is currently a *crisis*, not yet a 'Big Six' equivalent. **Barnosky et al. 2011** *Nature*: at current rates, the modern extinction will match the Big Five only if current rates continue for several centuries; with recovery (or further acceleration), the trajectory is uncertain. **Pimm + Joppa + Raven + Sodhi 2018** *Science*: estimated ~1 million species at risk, of ~10 million extant.

**Paleo-lessons for the 6th extinction**:
1. Recovery takes Myrs — far beyond human policy timescales.
2. **Heterogeneous** loss (some clades hit hard, others lightly) leaves persistent ecological scars.
3. **Top predators + large body sizes + specialists** are most vulnerable.
4. **Habitat connectivity + size** (MacArthur-Wilson) matter for survival.
5. **Climate-extinction synergies** are real — the Permian-Triassic example shows how rapid CO₂ + temperature changes amplify other stressors.
6. **Extinction debts** (committed but unrealized extinctions in fragmented habitats) play out over decades-centuries.
7. **Once it's gone, it's gone** — de-extinction can recover partial proxies but not true ancient species + ecosystems.

Mass extinctions are the most dramatic events in Earth's history + the most relevant deep-time analog for the Anthropocene. Next: **the vertebrate fossil record** — the lineages that produced us.

question.question: Compute the extinction-rate excess at the K-Pg boundary
question.goal: Estimate how many times above background extinction rate the K-Pg event represents.

steps.prompt: Background marine extinction rate ≈ 1 species per million species-years (E/MSY, Pimm). At K-Pg, ~75% of marine species went extinct in ~30 kyr. If the marine species count was ~5 × 10⁴ pre-K-Pg, what was the K-Pg extinction *rate* in E/MSY?
steps.reveal: Extinctions: $0.75 \times 5 \times 10^4 = 3.75 \times 10^4$ species over $3 \times 10^4$ yr → rate of $1.25$ species/yr. Per million species-years: $1.25 / (5 \times 10^4) \times 10^6 = 25{,}000$ E/MSY.

K-Pg extinction rate was ~25,000× background. This is the deep-time signature of a true mass extinction — orders of magnitude above noise. By comparison, the modern (Anthropocene) extinction rate is ~100-1000× background — concerning + accelerating but not yet at K-Pg intensity. Continuation of current trends for centuries would close that gap.

steps.prompt: Compute the modern extinction rate if we lose 1 million species (of 10 million) over 500 yr.
steps.reveal: Extinctions: $10^6$ over 500 yr → $2 \times 10^3$ species/yr. Per MSY: $2000 / (10^7) \times 10^6 = 200$ E/MSY. About 200× background — *severe* but ~125× below K-Pg. If extended over millennia, the 6th extinction would rival the Big Five. The question of timescale is critical: today's rate vs. fossil-record averages, vs. brief-pulse rates within mass extinctions.

acceptedAnswers: Even moderate extinction over millennia produces a Big Six; recovery takes Myr

steps.reveal: Paleo lesson: (1) Even a 'moderate' extinction sustained over centuries-millennia produces a Big-Six-scale event. (2) Recovery to pre-event diversity takes 5-30 Myr — far beyond human timescales. (3) Mass extinctions disproportionately affect large + slow-reproducing + specialist + top-predator species — exactly the categories currently threatened. (4) Mass-extinction events restructure ecospace (Bambach-Bush-Knoll) + favor disaster taxa (rats, cockroaches, jellyfish as candidates) over diverse + specialized faunas. (5) The window to avoid Big Six closes within decades. Paleontology supplies the most rigorous deep-time framework for thinking about modern biodiversity policy.

question.question: What is the **Alvarez hypothesis** for K-Pg + what evidence confirmed it?
options: **Alvarez et al. 1980** *Science* (Walter Alvarez geologist UC Berkeley + Luis Alvarez physicist Nobel 1968 + Frank Asaro + Helen Michel) proposed that the K-Pg extinction (66.0 Mya) was caused by a large asteroid impact. Evidence: (1) a **global iridium anomaly** (~30× background) in a thin clay layer at the K-Pg boundary worldwide — iridium is rare in Earth's crust but common in meteorites; (2) **shocked quartz** + microspherules at the same level; (3) **tsunami deposits** in Caribbean K-Pg sections; (4) consistency with the timing + magnitude of the extinction. Confirmation came from **Alan Hildebrand** et al. **1991** *Geology* + 1992 — identified the **Chicxulub crater** under the Yucatán Peninsula, ~180-200 km diameter, dated to 66.0 Mya. The structure had been mapped earlier by Pemex geophysicists (Penfield + Camargo 1981) but its impact origin was confirmed by Hildebrand. **Schulte et al. 2010** *Science* — 41-author consensus paper reviewing all evidence; concluded Chicxulub impact was the principal cause. The **Tanis site** (DePalma 2019 *PNAS* in Hell Creek) preserves a Lagerstätte of organisms killed within hours of the impact — including dinosaurs + fish with impact spherules in their gills. The **Deccan Traps** flood basalts (India, ~67-65 Mya) added climate stress; modern view: Chicxulub was the proximate cause, Deccan an aggravating factor.
question.explanation: Alvarez 1980: K-Pg extinction caused by asteroid impact; evidence = global iridium anomaly, shocked quartz, tsunami deposits. Hildebrand 1991 identified Chicxulub crater (Yucatán, 180-200 km, 66.0 Mya). Schulte 2010 41-author consensus confirmed. Tanis site (DePalma 2019) preserves victims killed within hours of impact. Deccan Traps added climate stress; Chicxulub was the proximate cause.

slides.workedSolution: Alvarez et al. 1980 proposed asteroid impact based on global iridium anomaly + shocked quartz. Hildebrand 1991 confirmed Chicxulub crater (Yucatán, 180-200 km, 66.0 Mya). Schulte 2010 consensus + Tanis site clinched the case. Deccan Traps contributed but Chicxulub was primary cause. Standard model of K-Pg extinction.

question.question: Comparing PT + K-Pg + Anthropocene as a paleontologist
question.prompt: You're writing a review comparing the three best-understood extinction events: the **Permian-Triassic 'Great Dying'** (252 Mya, Siberian Traps), the **K-Pg** (66 Mya, Chicxulub impact + Deccan), + the **ongoing 6th extinction**. Address: (1) the causal signature of each — how do volcanic + impact + anthropogenic causes differ in their kill mechanisms (warming, anoxia, acidification, dust, fragmentation)?; (2) the magnitudes + functional consequences — which guilds + clades disappear at each, + how does ecospace (Bambach-Bush-Knoll) reorganize?; (3) the recovery dynamics — Lystrosaurus + ferns + early mammals as disaster taxa; how do dead clades walking + ecospace refilling differ across events?; (4) the timescales — 60 kyr for PT, hours-decades for K-Pg, ongoing for 6th; (5) the analogs — what does PT teach about climate-driven extinction, what does K-Pg teach about catastrophic events, + which is the better analog for the 6th?; (6) the policy implications — what should the paleo evidence (recovery times of 5-30 Myr, IUCN Red List, Pimm-Brooks 100-1000× rates, Dirzo-Galetti defaunation, Zalasiewicz Anthropocene) tell us about urgency + intervention?; (7) the open questions — Schweitzer/Asara molecular evidence, Bailleul cellular preservation in PT survivors, de-extinction (Colossal mammoth, thylacine), and the long-term planetary trajectory.

question.question: The Permian-Triassic extinction lasted ~60 kyr (Burgess + Bowring 2014) + killed ~96% of marine species. If pre-PT marine species count was ~3 × 10⁴, what was the average extinction rate in **species per year**?
question.hint: Species lost = $0.96 \times 3 \times 10^4 = 2.88 \times 10^4$; rate = $2.88 \times 10^4 / 6 \times 10^4$ yr ≈ **0.48 species/yr**. Sustained over 60 kyr, this would be ~480,000× background (1 species per Myr per species). The end-Permian is the most catastrophic extinction in the Phanerozoic record.

question.prompt: In ≤140 words, summarize the Big Five mass extinctions + their recovery dynamics + the 6th extinction.
question.rubric: Mentions: **Raup + Sepkoski 1982** identified Big Five: **End-Ordovician** (~445 Mya, glaciation, ~85% spp), **Late Devonian** (~372 Mya, anoxia + Hangenberg, ~75%), **End-Permian** (~252 Mya, Siberian Traps + climate, **96% marine**, biggest ever; **Erwin** 2015), **End-Triassic** (~201 Mya, CAMP, ~70%), **K-Pg** (66 Mya, **Chicxulub impact** — Alvarez et al. 1980 + Hildebrand 1991 confirmation + Schulte 2010 review; Deccan accompaniment; ~75%, all non-avian dinosaurs). Recovery: **disaster taxa** (Lystrosaurus post-PT, ferns post-K-Pg), **dead clades walking** (Jablonski 2002 — brachiopods, crinoids post-PT), 5-30 Myr to full diversity (Erwin). Recovery is biased toward novel evolutionary types — Cenozoic mammals post-K-Pg, Mesozoic marine reptiles post-PT. **6th extinction**: **Pimm + Brooks** ~100-1000× background rates; **IUCN Red List** ~28% spp threatened; **Dirzo + Galetti 2014** vertebrate defaunation; **Zalasiewicz + AWG Anthropocene** proposal (voted down March 2024, informal use continues). Paleo-lesson: recovery takes Myr; window to avoid Big Six closes within decades.
